title: Why this sphere exists
summary: Python figures disproportionately in LLM training corpora, so LLM-authored Python is confident and plausible on the outside while quietly wrong on semantics an LLM does not memorise well: what is mutable and shared, when a value is None, which exception class a call can raise, how a splice should preserve untouched bytes. This sphere is deliberately portable and reference-style: each guide states the real Python semantics and the correct form it follows, so an authoring LLM can reproduce good code without relying on memorised snippets.
evidence_note: PLABEL: canonical/reference. Guidance here is grounded in the CPython data model and standard-library semantics, not in any single incident, because Python is a secondary surface of this project. Where a rule is statically detectable it is recorded as a rule document; where it requires reading what a call can do or what the author intends, it is an article.
invariants: A rule document states a deterministic trigger and a concrete correction, so it can be read and applied reliably.
An article carries the semantics and is used when intent or call behaviour must be decided.
Nothing here is a memory-claimer about an API's signature; statements about the language are the semantics, which do not drift by deployment.
